What are the best foods for healthy weight gain?

Start with familiar meals, add a protein source, include a starchy carbohydrate, and raise energy with foods such as nuts, seeds, cheese, avocado, olive oil, dairy or suitable alternatives. Use snacks or nourishing drinks when larger portions are difficult.
Energy and an easy base for meals
Eggs, fish, meat, beans, tofu, dairy
Nuts, seeds, olive oil, avocado, cheese
More calories without a much larger volume
Yogurt, nut butter toast, hummus and pita
Add calories to meals you already eat

The NHS suggests adding foods such as cheese, nuts and seeds to meals. NHS dietetic guidance also gives practical examples such as adding olive or rapeseed oil during cooking, using yogurt or cheese in dishes, and combining cereals with milk, fruit, nuts and seeds.

Small additions are easier to repeat than a completely new diet. Add nut butter to toast, olive oil to a rice bowl, cheese to eggs or pasta, or yogurt and nuts beside breakfast. Account for allergies, intolerances and dietary restrictions.
When appetite is the limiting factor

Large meals are not the only route. Eating smaller meals more often, adding two or three nourishing snacks and using higher-calorie drinks between meals can increase intake with less pressure at one sitting. Avoid filling up on drinks immediately before a meal if that reduces appetite.
Do not turn “high calorie” into “anything goes”

The NHS advises against relying on chocolate, cakes and sugary drinks for weight gain. Diet quality still matters. Include fruits and vegetables, vary protein sources, and use a mixture of carbohydrate and fat sources rather than building the entire surplus from one type of food.

Match the advice to your health

Generic food lists may be inappropriate for diabetes, kidney disease, digestive conditions, food allergies or other medical needs. Sudden or unintentional weight loss should be assessed rather than treated only by adding calories.

children: How large should your calorie surplus be for muscle gain?

A sustained surplus can support muscle gain and resistance-training demands, but the best starting amount is not the largest amount you can tolerate. Begin conservatively, train consistently, and use your weight trend to decide whether the target needs to move.
Published by Kestora Labs, the maker of BulkBro · Updated
How large should your calorie surplus be for muscle gain?

For adults, an extra 300–500 calories per day is a commonly cited general starting range for gradual weight gain. Muscle-focused lifters may choose a smaller percentage-based surplus, especially with more training experience. Neither approach guarantees a specific amount of muscle.
Start with an estimate you can test

The surplus is the difference between the energy you consume and the energy you use. Both sides are estimates in everyday life. A calculator can give you a practical maintenance target, but it cannot measure your metabolism directly or predict how your activity changes from week to week.

The NHS suggests that adults seeking gradual weight gain could try adding around 300–500 calories a day. An off-season bodybuilding review proposed a hyper-energetic diet of roughly 10–20% above maintenance, with advanced athletes being more conservative. These ranges come from different populations and should be treated as starting frameworks, not interchangeable prescriptions.
A surplus supports the process; training directs it

The International Society of Sports Nutrition states that diets focused on increasing lean mass are driven by a sustained calorie surplus that supports anabolic processes and greater resistance-training demands. The magnitude and composition of the surplus, as well as training status, influence the nature of the gain.

Calories alone do not provide the training stimulus. A muscle-focused plan also needs progressive resistance training, enough recovery and adequate protein. If strength training is absent, “muscle-gain surplus” becomes an inaccurate description of the goal.
Why a larger surplus is not automatically better

A small 2023 trial compared maintenance, moderate and high energy-surplus groups in resistance-trained participants. Faster body-mass gain primarily predicted increased skinfold thickness rather than consistently better muscle-thickness or strength outcomes. The sample was limited, but the result fits a practical concern: muscle gain has a limited rate, while surplus energy can also be stored as fat.

Use enough comparable weigh-ins to see direction without treating each reading as a verdict. For many adults, several morning readings or one consistent weekly check-in can work. The best routine is the one you can repeat calmly and interpret over time.
Published by Kestora Labs, the maker of BulkBro · Updated
How often should you weigh yourself while bulking?

Weigh at least consistently enough to compare one period with the next. Use the same scale, similar clothing and a similar time—commonly after waking and using the bathroom, before eating or drinking. Judge the trend, not the latest number.
Pick a routine before picking a frequency

A daily reading taken under changing conditions may be less useful than a weekly reading taken consistently. NHS guidance for recording weight emphasizes the same time of day and similar clothing. Keep the scale on the same firm surface and record the measurement rather than relying on memory.
Use the same scale and location.
Measure at a similar time of day.
Note unusual meals, travel or training when they add context.
Do not change the calorie target because of one reading.
Why body weight moves from day to day

Food and fluid in the body, hydration, sodium, carbohydrate intake and measurement timing can all affect short-term scale weight. Research has measured normal day-to-day variability even under standardized conditions. That is why a trend needs repeated observations or consistent weekly comparisons.
Daily, several times a week or weekly?

Research on self-weighing mostly concerns weight loss or prevention of weight gain, not intentional muscle-focused gain, so it does not establish one ideal bulking frequency. Daily or several-times-weekly data can make short-term variability visible. A consistent weekly check-in is simpler and may be sufficient for a weekly decision loop.

Choose the lowest frequency that still gives you enough evidence to interpret the plan. If you weigh daily, use an average or trend. If you weigh weekly, be especially consistent about timing and conditions.
Weighing should not control the day

Reduce the frequency or stop if weighing causes anxiety, compulsive checking, restrictive behavior or distress. People with a history of disordered eating should follow guidance from an appropriate healthcare professional rather than a generic tracking routine.

Why am I not gaining weight?

Your planned calorie surplus may not be the surplus you actually completed, your starting maintenance estimate may be off, or short-term body-weight variation may be hiding the direction of change. Use a complete week of intake and consistently timed weigh-ins before making a measured adjustment.
Work through the evidence in order

A calorie target is an estimate. Your completed logs and weight response show whether that estimate fits you. Changing several parts of the plan at once makes it harder to learn what worked, so check each part of the loop before reacting.
1. Check whether the starting target makes sense

Most calorie calculators estimate resting energy needs and apply a broad activity factor. They do not directly measure your personal maintenance calories. A useful target can therefore be slightly too high, too low or close enough to test.

2. Compare the target with what you actually ate

A target of 3,000 calories does not create a surplus if completed logs average 2,650. Use the average of the days you actually logged, and check whether missing meals, drinks, snacks or unfinished days make that average unreliable.
